演奏鋼鼓時，以直槌敲擊鼓面音區發聲；槌頭包橡膠，大小與類型依所奏音域調整。初學可: The steel drum is played by striking the note areas of its face with straight sticks whose tips are wrapped in rubber; the size and type of stick follow the register being played. Begin by learning the layout of the note areas: the larger the area, the lower the pitch, and the length of the skirt goes with treble or bass. The basic order is: hold the sticks, aim at the note area, strike with the tip. Some players hold two sticks in each hand to control more note areas at once; when playing several steel drums, the player has to divide the hands between registers.

鋼鼓主要出現在千里達及托巴哥嘉年華的打擊樂編制中，由坦布竹傳統演變而來，以成對橡: The steel drum appears mainly in the percussion sections of Trinidad and Tobago's carnival. It developed out of the tamboo bamboo tradition and sounds when a pair of straight sticks with rubber tips strike the face of a steel barrel; it is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241.2. Whole steel bands have played on international occasions such as the Festival of Britain, the Commonwealth Arts Festival and the Montreal world's fair, have toured with Liberace, and have been used on Broadway stages; the modern steel drum is a chromatic percussion instrument that can take the lead, the bass or an ensemble part.
鋼鼓源自千里達及托巴哥，由西非會話鼓經跨大西洋奴隸貿易傳入，並在1785年起當地: The steel drum comes from Trinidad and Tobago: it arrived with West African talking drums through the transatlantic slave trade and took shape in local carnival and underground celebrations from 1785 onwards. After African percussion was banned in the 1880s, players turned to tamboo bamboo; metal percussion was added in the 1930s, and in 1937 Laventille saw a band made of pots, dustbin lids and oil drums. In 1941 the American forces stationed on the island helped it go international, the 1951 Festival of Britain performance made the steel drum famous, in 1992 Prime Minister Patrick Manning declared it the national instrument, and in 2023 the United Nations set 11 August as World Steelpan Day.
鋼鼓為體鳴樂器，主體由工業用鋼製油桶敲製而成，來源提到現代鋼鼓以200公升工業桶: The steel drum is an idiophone whose body is hammered out of an industrial steel oil drum; the source notes that modern steel drums are made from 200-litre industrial barrels, while earlier ones used 55-gallon oil drums. The cylindrical part of the barrel is called the skirt, and its length varies with the register. The face is tuned into note areas of different sizes, and the surface may be painted, chrome-plated, nickel-plated, powder-coated or hardened. The playing sticks are straight, with rubber-wrapped tips, sized and shaped according to the register of the instrument. The source does not state the materials of the remaining parts.
鋼鼓音色明亮溫暖，具有獨特的金屬共鳴質感。其音域寬廣，通常涵蓋兩至三個八度，從低: The steel drum is bright and warm, with a distinctive metallic resonance. Its range is wide, usually two to three octaves, from a deep bass to a clear treble. Because the face is shaped into hollows, striking different areas gives different pitches, so the tone has many layers. It resonates in its own way: every stroke produces a warm, penetrating sound with a slight ring trailing after it. Compared with traditional drums, the steel drum is closer to the clarity of a xylophone or metallophone, but its resonating body is warmer; compared with the piano, it has more of a metallic sheen and a tropical character, creating a cheerful, lively atmosphere.

The steel drum (steelpan, also called pan) is an idiophone from Trinidad and Tobago, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241.2. Modern steel drums are mostly made from 200-litre industrial oil drums, and the face is tuned so that it can play chromatic pitches; the pitch of a note area goes with the length of the skirt, a treble instrument holding several dozen notes while a bass one may have only three. Players are called pannists, and they usually strike with a pair of straight sticks with rubber tips, changing the tips according to the type of drum; some also hold two sticks in each hand. It grew out of the early carnival percussion tradition, is now the national instrument of Trinidad and Tobago, and appears on the national coat of arms.
